case_source: From the judgment and order dated 14.2.1977 passed by the High Court in Civil Revision Case No. 1696 of 1968.
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam, J.—This appeal by special Ism arises from the judgment dated February 14 1977 of the High Court of Bangladesh in Civil Revision Case No. 1696 of 1968 in connection with the pre-emption case under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.

2. The short question for consideration In this appeal it whether the learned Single Judge of the High Court correctly appreciated the ratio decidendt of the decision of this Court in Motilal Sikder vs. Benodini Dasi, 28 DLR (AD) 5, and whether the same has been correctly applied to the facts and circumstances of this case.

3. Facts relevant for disposal of the appeal are that the pre-emptor respondent No. 1 filed an application claiming to be a co-sharer in the holding and prayed for pre-emption of the transfer of .45 acres of land dated October 25, 1965 made by respondent No. 3 Abdul Huq Sarker in favour of the appellants who are strangers to the holding, at Taka 1000/- without serving notice of the sale. The pre-emptor respondent claimed that he came to know about the sale on October 30, 1965 and filed the pre-emption case on February 23, 1966. The appellants contested the case by filing two sets of written objection contending, inter alia, that the case Is not maintainable on account of defect of parties, as many of the co-sharers by inheritance in the case holding have not been impleaded. They further contended that they are not the actual purchasers but they are the benamdars of their mother Afronnessa who being a co-sharer by inheritance in the holding made the purchase in the benami of her minor sons, and, as such, the sale cannot be made subject-matter of pre-emption. Their further case is that the original holding was never auction-sold nor any fresh settlement was taken by the original tenants and no fresh or separate holding was created in respect of the case land.

4. The pre-emption case was allowed by the Munsif, Jamalpur, and on appeal by the appellants, the judgment was reversed by the Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Mymensingh. The learned Subordinate Judge held that the pre-emption case was not maintainable in the absence of some of the co-sharers by Inheritance. On a revisional application filed by the pre-emptor-respondent under section 113 of the Code of Civil Procedure the learned Single Judge of the High Court of Bangladesh set aside the judgment of the lower Appellate Court holding that the pre-emption case should not be dismissed on the ground of non-joinder of necessary parties. It is not necessary that all the co-sharers of the holding should be impleaded in the pre-emption proceeding. In taking this view the learned Judge referred to the decision In Motilal Sikder vs. Benodini Dasi. The learned Judge held that the provision of sub-section (2) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 regarding parties to the proceeding is directory, and not mandatory; and, as such, the pre-emption application was not bad for defect of parties. On this view the judgment of lower Appellate Court was set aside.

5. From the judgment of the learned Single Judge it appears that he agreed with the finding of the lower Appellate Court that some co-sharers by inheritance in the holding were omitted from the proceeding, but he condoned this defect on the ground that the requirement with regard to the making of parties in a pre-emption proceeding as provided in sub-section (2) of section 96 of the Act is directory and omission of some of the co-sharers from the proceeding cannot be fatal to the same. The learned Judge quoted certain passage from the decision in Motilal Sikder vs. Benodini Dasi which runs as under:

"It does not appear from a perusal of the provisions of section 96 that it was the intent of the legislature that the penalty for non-impleading a person as contemplated in sub-section (2) Is the invalidity of the order which may ultimately be made in the said proceeding. The question whether a person re a necessary party under sub-section (2) is a question of fact and the object of this provision seems to provide the co-sharer tenants and the holders to the contiguous lands with the opportunity of availing of the provision of the said sub-section. Since the benefit conferred under the said provision is meant for certain individuals, they can very well of waived. In that view of the matter the positive injunction contained in the said sub section as to the making of parties in spite of its being couched in mandatory language, should be read as directory".

6. Mr. Akram Hossein Amin, the learned Advocate on Record appearing for the appellants submitted that the learned Single Judge of the High Court failed to make proper appreciation of the ratio decidendt of the judgment in Motilal Sikder Vs. Benodini Dasi. He elaborated his submission stating that the observations made in the decision or Motilal Sikder Vs. Benodini Dasi do not give the indication that their Lordships were taking the view that the provision as contained in sub-section (2) of section 96 regarding making parties In a pre-emption case is directory and not mandatory.

7. On perusal of the judgment in Motilal Sikder Vs. Benodini Dasi it appears that in the context of the facts and circumstances of that case the following observation has been made:

"Since the benefit conferred under the said provision is meant for certain Individual, they can very well be waived. In that view of the matter the positive injunction contained in the said sub-section as to the making of parties In spite of its being couched in mandatory language, should be read as directory."

8. For proper appreciation of the ratio decidendi of the said decision in Motilal Sikder Vs. benodini Dasi some facts of the case are necessary to be stated. An application for pre-emption under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was filed by the appellants claiming to be owners of the lands contiguous to the land sold by a registered kabala for consideration. The application was contested by the transferee contending, inter alia, that the applicants were not owners of contiguous lands; and that the application was not maintainable in the absence of contiguous land owners as named in the written objection. To meet this objection the appellants impleaded the persons whose names were supplied by the pre-emptee. At that trial only two points were pressed, namely whether the petitioners were the owners of the contiguous lands and whether the application was barred by limitation. On both the points the learned Munsif found, on consideration of the evidence, in favour of the pre-emptors. On the question of defect of partied the learned Munsif observed:

"An objection as to the defect of parties was stated in the written objection but the same was not pressed".

9. On appeal the decision was affirmed by the Subordinate Judge. No objection as to the defect of parties was canvassed before the said Court at the hearing of the rule issued on a revisional application filed by the pre-emptee. An application was filed on behalf of the pre-emptee praying for consideration of an additional ground which was as under: For that the Courts below acted without jurisdiction in allowing pre-emption that the preemption case is not duty constituted due to want of impleading of necessary parties as on showing all the pre-emptors by Exhibit 1 (e)."

10. The learned Single Judge allowed the petitioners to urge the additional round. II was contended that one Mozaffar Ali Khan who happened to be the co-purchaser with one Ledu Khan in the kabala Exhibit 1(b) by which the said Ledu Khan claimed to have acquired interest in the land contiguous to the land under pre-emption, and as such the said Mozaffar Ali Khan was a necessary party, in whose absence the application for pre-emption was not maintainable. The learned Single Judge relying upon the decision of a Division Reach of the Dacca High Court in Syed Abdul Karim vs. Harendra Chanara Dhupi. 14 D L.R 847, accepted the contention and dismissed the application for per emption. Special leave to appeal was granted to the appellants to consider whether cue objection chat Mozzaffar Ali Khan was a necessary party which was taken for the first time in the High Court should have been entertained and whether in any view of the matter the case should have been remanded for Investigation whether he was a necessary party.

11. While considering the ground upon which the leave was granted his Lordship observed that the question of joinder of partner is essentially a matter of procedure and some detailed rules have been provided in the Code of Civil Procedure. On the question of joinder of parties, in the course of discussion of this question, his Lordship observed that Order I of the Code of Civil Procedure deals with the question of the parties to a suit and by virtue of section 141 of the Code, the said provisions are applicable to a proceeding of original nature like the one under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The discussion, however, mainly centred on the rules of pleading which provide that any objection as to the maintainability of a suit which requires investigation of acts must be taken in the pleading before the framing of the issues. So that the other party may not be taken by surprise and is prejudiced in the matter of taking steps to meet the objection. According to his Lordship the principle relating to a partition suit has got no application to a proceeding for pre-emption His Lords ship referred to a decision of a Single Judge of the High Court in the care of Syed Abdul Karim vs. Harendre Cnandra Dhupi, 14 DLR 847 which contains the following observation:

"In the case of pre-emption because of the special provision of the Act, rights of the parties cannot be deter-mined without considering the right of others. The principle of Order 1, rule 9 of the Code cannot be made applicable. In the circumstances, it cannot be said that the tenants holding lands contiguous to lands transferred are not necessary parties as they are persons whose presence is necessary for the proper constitution of the pre-emption application, Their presence is not only a matter of convenience but of absolute necessity to enable the Court to adjudicate more effectively and completely. Order 1, rule 9 of the Code does not apply when a cause of action arises against a number of persons jointly because when one of such persons is eliminated no cause of action subsists against other as in the suit for partition. In the case of preemption under section 96 of the Act, the cause of action arises not only against the transferee but also against the co-sharer and other holders of contiguous lands".

12. According to his Lordship the analogy drawn in the above noted decision between a suit for partition and the proceeding for pre-emption does not appear to be based on sound reasoning. His Lordship however approved another principle laid down in the said decision with the following observation:

"It should, however, be noticed that in the said case reported in 14 DLR 847 the Dacca High Court laid down another principle which appears to be substantially correct. Reading sub-sections (2) and (4) of section 96 together, the said Court took the view that only those of the co-sharer tenants and the holders of contiguous lands, whose right of pre-emption had not been barred under subs section (1) of section 96 were necessary parties within the meaning of sub-section (2) of the said section. Although we have been unable to concur in the other view expressed in the said case as to the analogy between a suit for partition and the proceeding for pre-emption, but the aforesaid principle as to a necessary party in a proceeding for pre-emption has been, in our opinion, correctly pronounced. From sub-section (4) of section 96 it Is clear that the said provision was obviously made for the purpose of providing the facility of pre-emption to the persons interested, who have not lost their right of pre-emption under sub-section (1) of the said section"

13. The above quotations provide sufficient indication as to the manner how the appeal under consideration was disposed of. The petitioners were allowed to take an additional ground showing defect of party at the hearing of the rule which was not taken at the trial of the pre-emption case and objection on the ground of non-joinder of necessary parties was not pressed at the trial. The pre-emption application was dismissed only on accepting the objection which was taken for the first time in revision and without sending the case back to the trial Court to find out as to whether the said persons omitted from the proceeding had any subsisting interest in the land as shown by the pre-emptee. The uncontroverted statement of the appellants made in respect of the subsisting interest of Mozaffar Ali Khan was accepted. It was stated that there was a subsequent partition of the lands purchased by Exhibit 1 (b) between the two brothers and the portion which fell in the share of Ledu Khan was contiguous to the land under pre-emption and the portion which was allotted to Mozaffar Ali Khan was not contiguous to the said lands. In this background the appeal was allowed and judgment of the High Court was set aside and the judgment of the Courts below were restored.

14. With one respect I must say that the above noted opinion that the positive injunction contained in sub-section (2) of section 96 as to making parties is to be read as directory and not mandatory as its language indicates, is limited to the particular facts of the case.

Sub-section (2) of section 96 reads as under:

“In an application made under subs section (1) by a co-sharer tenant or co-sharer tenants, all other co-sharer tenants of the holding and the transferee shell be made parties and in such an application made by a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred, all the co-sharer tenants of the holding and all the tenants holding lauds contiguous to the land transferred and the transferee shall be made parties"

<u>15. The right of pre-emption as provided under sub-section (1) of section 96 is a statutory right. The cause of action for pre-emption of any transfer accrues to the co-sharer tenants and contiguous land owners This right of the applicant or applicant claiming to be cc-sharer tenants or owner of contiguous land, is not absolute but subject to the right of other co sharers and other holders of land contiguous to the land transferred, as the case may be, for proper adjudication. To give fall effect to the statutory provision, all the necessary parties must be impleaded, because relief cannot be given in the absence of such party.</u>

<u>16. The right to purchase the land transferred as contemplated under section 96 is a statutory right and it is to be exercised within 4 months of the service of notice under section 89, or if no notice has been served under section 89, within four months of the date of knowledge of the transfer. The right to purchase the land has been very clearly and unambiguously spelt out by the legislature in the section. The language of the provisions in different parts of the section shows that the right to purchase conferred upon the co-sharer tenants or the contiguous land owners is not by any means dependent upon initiation of the pre-emption proceeding either by a co-sharer tenant or owner of the land contiguous to the land of transfer. However, the section does not cast any duty upon the Court to find out through process of enquiry all the non-notified co-sharers if any or all the non-impleaded contiguous land owners, and for complete adjudication implead them In the proceedings, Sub-section (2) requires that all the co-sharer tenants of the holding are to be impleaded in the application failing under the first part of sub-section (1). Similarly, all the contiguous land owners are to be made parties in the application failing under the second part of sub-section (1), Sab-section (4) provides the period of limitation for the remaining co-sharer tenant or the tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred, to join in the pre-emption proceedings. This period of two months begins to run from the service of notice of the application for pre-emption. The different provisions of section 96 clearly point out that a duty has been cast upon the pre-emptor, if he is a co-sharer tenant, to make all the remaining co-sharer tenants, and if he is a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred, all the remaining tenants boiling lands contiguous to the land transferred and the transferee, parties to the application. Object of sub-section (2) is to have all the co-sharer tenants or all the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred, before the Court for proper and complete adjudication in accordance with law. A co-sharer tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred may waive his right to purchase the land, but on this consideration there is hardly any scope for taking the view that the requirement of sub-section (2) is not mandatory but is me rely directory. Second Part of sub-section (4) clearly indicates that a co-sharer tenant or a tenant having land contiguous to the land transferred failing to join in the pre-emption proceeding within the given time, shall not have any further right to purchase under this section. Waive of the right is one thing, but defeating the right by deliberate omission in the pre-emption application is a different thing. There is hardly any scope to doubt that the clear object, of legislation is that all the parties having right of pre-emption should be before the Court for adjudication of the right or rights of pre-emption in accordance with law.</u>

17. Now the question is whether the omission of any necessary party in the pre-emption proceeding entails automatic failure of the proceeding. In Motilal Sikder Vs. Benodini Dasi an attempt has been made to lay down the principal that the provision as contained in sub-section (2) of section 96 is not mandatory but merely directory, in other words, no duty cast upon the pre-emptor to implead all the parties who are, as contemplated under section 96, necessary parties. This view is mere founded on the provision of procedure as provided under Order 1, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure than strict interpretation of the language of the section.

18. The procedure with regard to misjoinder and non-joinder of parties in a suit or a proceeding in any Court of civil jurisdiction, in view of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure, Order 1. rule 9 is applicable. Order 1, rule 9 reads as under:—

"No suit shall be defeated by reason of the misjoinder or non-joinder of parties, and the Court may in every suit deal with the matter in controversy so far as regards the rights and interest of the parties actually before it."

<u>19. The question of non-joinder of necessary party affecting framing of a pre-emption application is to be decided keeping in view the requirement of the different sub-sections of section 96 along with the provisions as contained in Order 1, rules 9 and 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, because, Pre-emption proceedings being one of the proceedings as contemplated under section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure the procedure of law in Order I, rule 9 is applicable. On account of omission of necessary party a preemption case shall not be dismissed outright keeping In view the provision of Order 1, role 9, inasmuch as non-joinder of necessary party will not by itself defeat a suit proceeding However, the special statutory provision in sub-section (2) as to the necessary parties to be impleaded is mandatory. In clear language it mentions the persons to be impleaded in an application made under sub-section (1) by a co-sharer tenant: and in an application made by a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred. Requirement of the statutory provision cannot be minimised by the procedural law as contained in Order 1, rule 9. The special provision in sub section (2) is not controlled by Order 1, rule 9, which merely provides that a suit shall not be dismissed by reason of mere non-joinder of necessary parties. Order 1, rule 10 provides for addition of party at any stage of the proceedings, either upon or without the application of either party. Where there is non-joinder of a necessary party the Court is ems powered to add the necessary party under rule 10 at any stage of the proceeding, either upon or without the application of either party. The objection as to non-joinder of necessary parties must be taken at the earliest opportunity by the defendant. Such objection provides an opportunity to the plains tiff to remove the defect by adding parties who were omitted. In taking objection on the ground of non-joinder of necessary parties the defendant is required to furnish the names and particulars of the parties who were omitted from the suit. On the refusal of the plaintiff to implead the parties mentioned in the written statement, the question becomes an issue for adjudication by the Court and on adjudication the question becomes decided. In such an event the consequences must follow, that is, the suit becomes liable to be dismissed on the ground of non-joinder of necessary party. In the case of a pre-emption preceding the law regarding procedure cannot be treated as different. If the pre-emptee or for that matter any of the parties disclose existence of a necessary party and furnishes the necessary particulars, but the pre-emptor still insists not to implead him as a party, consequence on adjudication is the same. It has already been mentioned that such objection regarding non-joinder of necessary parties should be taken at the earlier opportunity, before the trial, because an enquiry on this question may be necessary. Of course, in an appropriate case such objection may be allowed to be raised in the appeal. This may be done on the ground that the appeal is continuation of the suit or proceeding. But there is no scope for raising the question of defect of party on account of non-joinder of necessary parties, for the first time in revision.</u>

20. In the instant case written objection was filed by the appellants contending; inter alia, that the case was not maintainable due to defect of parties, as many of the co-sharers by inheritance in the holding were omitted. It was, inter-alia, stated that their mother Afronnessa who being herself one of such co-sharers by Inheritance In the holding was a necessary party, and In her absence the pre-emption case was liable to be dismissed. The learned Munsif overruling the objection allowed the pre-emption case with the following observation:

"In view of my finding in the foregoing pares I do not find any prima facie evidence to the effect that the said Afronnesse is a co-sharer of the holding. And these are serious , questions of title involved in this case in the way of determination of Afronnessa or anybody else named in w/s has any share in the case holding or not. And these questions cannot be decided in this Miscellaneous Case without properly being framed in title suit".

21. On appeal the main question for consideration was whether the application for pre-emption was maintainable or whether it was bad for defect of parties. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the materials on record found that the question was not properly adjudicated by the learned Munsif inasmuch as he based his decision upon a wrong assumption that the S.A. Record should be presumed to be correct and that there is no need of scrutiny as to its correctness. The learned Subordinate Judge found that some of the co-sharers by inheritance in the holding including the appellant's mother Afronnessa were not impleaded in the preemption case, although this objection was taken by she pre-emptees at the earliest opportunity. The learned Subordinate Judge after consideration of the evidence arrived at the following finding:

“Thus, upon the evidence on record I find that the case is legally not maintainable due to defect of parties as several co-sharers by inheritance have not been brought on record".

22. On the basis of the finding that several co-sharers in the holding were omitted in the pre-emption case and they were not brought on record in spite of objection taken by the pre-emptees in this respect, set aside the order of the Munsif and dismissed the pre-emption case.

23. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division however set aside the judgment of the lower Appellate. Court on taking the view that on account of defect of parties the case should not have been dismissed. He practically acted on the authority of the decision in Motilal Sikder vs. Benodini Dasi, wherein the following observation occurs:

"The expression a positive injunction contained in the said sub-section as to the making of parties in spite of its being couched in mandatory language should be read as directory".

24. The provision of law as contained to sub-section (2) should be followed without minimising its requirement. The requirement as to making of parties is undoubtedly positive. It is the duty of the pre-emptor to implead the necessary parties as I have already observed above that this requirement of law should be enforced keeping in view the provisions of Order 1, rules 9 and 10 if the prey emptor, after getting an opportunity, fails to amend his application by impleading the necessary parties as pointed out by the pre-emptee, and on evidence if it is found that the application suffers from defect of parties, in that event the application cannot succeed and must be dismissed. I fully agree with the view expressed in the case reported in 14 DLR 847 that presence of the persons mentioned in sub-section (2) of section 96 " is not only a matter of convenience but of absolute necessity to enable the Court to adjudicate more effectively and completely". Otherwise, a non-notified co-sharer or a contiguous land owner may have an occasion to challenge the decision and to try to re-open the matter. The decision in Motilal Sikder vs. Benodini Dasi, should be read in the light of the observations made above.

<u>25. The learned Single Judge while upsetting the decision of the lower Appellate Court omitted to notice that the pre-emption case was dismissed mainly on the ground that the pre-emptors failed to implead the necessary parties in spite of opportunity given to them by supplying the names in the written objection; and that on evidence it was found by the lower Appellate Court that the persons named in the written objection were co-sharers by inheritance having subsisting Interest in the holding, and In their absence the pre-emption case was not maintainable. The learned Judge in considering the question whether the sub-section (2) is directory or mandatory observed that non-inclusion of the persons named by the pre-emptees does not affect the application for pre-emption. "since the benefit of pre-emption is an individual opportunity and, as such, may be waived". Right to purchase a land may be waived, but that cannot be made a ground to relax the mandate of the statute to implead the necessary parties in the proceeding. A co-sharer in the holding cannot be allowed to purchase the entire land without impleading the other co-sharers and thereby depriving them from getting their share Similarly, a tenant owning land contiguous to the land transferred cannot be allowed to purchase the entire land transferred without impleading the other tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred, and thereby depriving them from exercising their right in the case of second category of pre-emptors presence of other tenants or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred is necessary for the purpose of determination of the order of priority as among the tenants in the manner as indicated in clause (b) of sub-section (5). So, presence of all the persons mentioned in sub-section (2), as the case may be, is more a matter of absolute necessity than of mere convenience. Their presence is necessary, so that the Court can adjudicate the claim of pre-emption more effectively and completely.</u>

26. In the instant case as I have already indicated above the pre-emptors got sufficient opportunity to remove the defect by impleading the persons named in the written objection but they failed to remove the defect, and, consequently, the application must be treated as not properly constituted. The pre-emptors cannot succeed on such an application. In that view of the matter the judgment of the learned Single Judge cannot be sustained, therefore, the appeal is allowed with costs and the judgment of the High Court set aside. Judgment and order of the lower Appellate Court are restored.

End.
